questions.q: The no-air model predicts 86 m/s; measurements say about 18 m/s. What's the right response?

opts.t: Trust the math; the experiments must be wrong
Go back to abstraction and add the missing physics (drag), then check again

questions.why: A failed validation tells you which simplification mattered. Here, ignoring air resistance was fine for a short drop but not for 381 m. Iterate: add drag, predict, validate again.

questions.q: Describe the modeling loop this course uses, with the penny as the example.
questions.a:
• Abstraction: decide what to include (gravity) and what to leave out (air).
  • Analysis/simulation: compute the prediction (86 m/s, 8.8 s).
  • Validation: compare with measurements (about 18 m/s), find the model is wrong.
  • Iterate: add the missing piece (drag), predict and validate again.

questions.q: What does "sweeping a parameter" mean, and why is it useful?
questions.a:
• Running the same model many times while varying one parameter over a range, and recording a metric for each value.
  • It shows how sensitive the results are to the parameter, finds ranges where the system works well or badly, and supports decisions (e.g. how many bikes to put at each station).

questions.title: The simulation loop
questions.tests: assert len(results) == 67 and abs(results[2016] - (2.558 + 66 * 0.0723)) < 1e-9

questions.q: The constant-growth line matches both ends but runs above the data around 1950–1970 and below it around 1990. What does that suggest?

opts.t: Growth per year wasn't constant: it was smaller early on and larger later

questions.why: Fitting the endpoints forces the line through them; the systematic misses in between tell you the real growth rate changed over time. Chapter 6 tries growth proportional to population.

questions.q: Describe the constant-growth model: how its one parameter is chosen and how the simulation works.
questions.a:
• Parameter: annual_growth = (p_end − p_0)/(t_end − t_0), chosen so the model matches the first and last data points.
  • Simulation: start with results[t_0] = p_0; for each year t, results[t+1] = results[t] + annual_growth.
  • It's a straight line; it misses the curvature in the data.

questions.why: Growth proportional to size compounds: each year's increase is bigger than the last. Real population growth has slowed since the 1960s, so the model must change; chapter 7 adds crowding.

questions.q: Why do we factor out the update function from run_simulation?
questions.a:
• The loop (start at p_0, step year by year, store results) is the same for every model; only the rule for next year changes.
  • Passing the rule as an argument lets one run_simulation work for constant, proportional and quadratic growth, so you can swap models without rewriting the loop and compare them fairly.

questions.title: Equilibrium two ways
questions.setup:
def update_func_quad(pop, t, system):
    return pop + system.alpha * pop + system.beta * pop**2
questions.tests:
assert abs(p_eq - 13.889) < 0.01, f"-alpha/beta is about 13.89, got {p_eq}"

questions.q: Starting above the carrying capacity, the population falls toward it; starting below, it rises toward it. What kind of equilibrium is that?

opts.t: Neutral: it stays wherever it starts

questions.why: If net growth is negative above the equilibrium and positive below, the system always moves back toward it: a stable equilibrium. p = 0 is the other equilibrium, and it's unstable.

questions.q: What's the equilibrium of the quadratic model, why does the model have one, and is it stable?
questions.a:
• Net growth alpha·p + beta·p² is zero at p = −alpha/beta (≈ 13.9 billion with these values).
  • Because beta < 0, crowding grows faster than births as p rises, so growth hits zero.
  • It's stable: above it net growth is negative, below it positive, so the population moves toward it.

questions.q: The fitted line slopes down. In terms of the model, what does that mean?

opts.t: beta is negative: the per-person growth rate falls as population rises

questions.why: A negative slope is a negative beta, the crowding term. The fit supports the quadratic model's key assumption, at least for these years.

questions.q: The quadratic model and the UN projection broadly agree to 2050, then drift apart. Which statement is fairest?

opts.t: The model proves the UN is wrong
The model shows one possible future if past trends continue; the UN uses much more detailed information (age structure, fertility trends), so agreement is reassuring but neither is certain
Long-range projections are impossible, so the model is useless
The models agree, so the future is known

questions.why: A simple model fitted to the past can only extend past trends. Its value is in making the assumptions explicit, and comparing it with expert projections shows where the extra detail matters.

questions.q: How do you estimate alpha and beta for the quadratic model from data?
questions.a:
• Compute the per-person growth rate between consecutive data points: Δp / Δt / p.
  • Plot it against population; the quadratic model predicts a straight line, rate = alpha + beta·p.
  • Fit a line (e.g. np.polyfit(p, rate, 1)): the intercept is alpha, the slope is beta.

questions.q: The simulation and the closed form are close but not identical. Why?

opts.t: The simulation takes one-year steps (a recurrence), while the closed form solves the continuous equation; smaller steps would bring them closer

questions.why: The yearly recurrence is an approximation to the differential equation. The difference is a discretization error, which shrinks as the time step shrinks.

questions.q: When would you use analysis rather than simulation, and vice versa?
questions.a:
• Analysis (closed-form solutions) gives insight into how results depend on parameters, and is fast for any time or input, but only exists for some models.
  • Simulation works for almost any model (nonlinear, random, complicated) but gives one numerical answer per run and less insight.
  • Check one against the other when both are possible.

questions.q: The two curves are surprisingly close: one queue is at best slightly better. Why can two queues do almost as well in this model?

opts.t: Arriving customers always join the shorter queue, which keeps the two lines balanced, so a counter rarely sits idle while the other line waits

questions.why: The advantage of one shared line is that no counter ever idles while someone is waiting. Joining the shorter line gets most of that benefit. Real customers can't see who will be slow and don't always choose well; the challenge below tests that.

questions.q: Explain Little's law and how the case study uses it.
questions.a:
• L = λ·W: the average number in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each customer spends there.
  • The simulation tracks only the number in the system each minute, so averaging that gives L, and W = L/λ gives the average wait without tracking individual customers.

questions.q: Why is the number of new infections proportional to s·i and not just to i?

opts.t: An infection needs a contact between an infectious person and a susceptible one; as susceptibles run out, contacts stop producing infections
Because recovered people get sick again

questions.why: Each infectious person's contacts are spread over the whole population, and only the fraction s of them can be infected. That s·i product is what eventually stops the epidemic.

questions.q: The epidemic ends with about half the class never infected. Why doesn't everyone get sick?

opts.t: The model runs out of days
As S falls, each infected person produces fewer new infections; once that drops below the recovery rate, infections die out while susceptibles remain
β is too small to infect anyone

questions.why: New infections are β·i·s. When s falls below γ/β, each case causes less than one new case on average, so the epidemic shrinks even though susceptible people remain. This is the idea behind herd immunity.

questions.title: How many got sick?
questions.tests: assert abs(total_infected - 0.468) < 0.005, f"About 47% of students get sick, got {total_infected:.3f}"

questions.q: Describe the SIR model: compartments, parameters, and the flow equations for one day.
questions.a:
• Compartments S, I, R as fractions of the population.
  • β: contact rate (infecting contacts per infected person per day); γ: recovery rate (1 / days sick).
  • Each day: infected = β·i·s moves from S to I; recovered = γ·i moves from I to R.
  • The total s + i + r stays 1.

questions.title: Sweep the vaccination rate
questions.tests:

questions.q: Vaccinating the first 10% prevents far more than 10% of infections. Why?

opts.t: Each vaccinated person is one fewer link in the chain, so they protect others too; near the threshold, small increases can stop the epidemic

questions.why: Removing susceptibles slows transmission for everyone (herd immunity). The curve is steepest at first and flattens once the epidemic is mostly prevented.

questions.q: The best split isn't "all vaccines" or "all hand washing". What modeling idea produces an interior optimum like this?

opts.t: Diminishing returns: the logistic campaign gives most of its benefit for the first few hundred dollars, so spending everything there wastes money that vaccines would use better

questions.why: When one option's benefit flattens out, the last dollar does more good elsewhere. The sweep finds where the marginal benefits balance.

questions.q: How does the model represent vaccination and hand washing, and how do we choose between them?
questions.a:
• Vaccination: move a fraction of the population from S to R before the start.
  • Hand washing: reduce β by a factor that depends on spending through a logistic (diminishing-returns) curve.
  • For each way of splitting the budget, run the simulation and compute total infected; sweep the split and pick the minimum.

questions.q: What is the contact number, why do SIR results depend only on it, and how can you estimate it?
questions.a:
• c = β/γ: infecting contacts per day times days infectious, i.e. new cases per case in a fully susceptible population.
  • Dividing the SIR equations removes time units; the shape of the outbreak (final size) depends only on the ratio.
  • From an observed final fraction of susceptibles s∞, c = ln(s∞)/(s∞ − 1).

questions.title: Cool a cup for 30 minutes

questions.q: A cup of coffee at 90 °C and one at 40 °C sit in a 22 °C room. Under Newton's law, which loses temperature faster right now, and by how much?

opts.t: The 40 °C cup, because it's closer to the room
Neither, until they touch something cold

questions.why: The rate is proportional to the temperature difference: 68 °C vs 18 °C. Hot things cool fast; the cooling slows as they approach room temperature.

questions.q: State Newton's law of cooling and explain how it becomes an update function.
questions.a:
• dT/dt = −r(T − T_env): cooling rate proportional to the temperature difference with the surroundings.
  • In discrete steps of length dt: T_next = T − r·(T − T_env)·dt.
  • r is fitted to a measurement (e.g. 70 °C after 30 min); the time step must multiply the rate.

questions.q: Why is adding the milk at the end the better choice for drinking hot coffee?

opts.t: Cooling is fastest when the coffee is hottest; mixing late keeps the coffee hot during the fast-cooling period, and the cold milk warms up meanwhile
It doesn't matter; both orders give the same answer

questions.why: Newton's law makes hot coffee lose heat faster. Keeping it at 90 °C longer means more loss, but the cold milk also gains heat from the room while it waits, and with these parameters that wins. The answer depends on the numbers, which is why we simulate.

questions.q: How do you use root finding to fit a model parameter to a measurement?
questions.a:
• Write an error function: given the parameter, run the model and return (model output − measurement).
  • Find a bracket where the error changes sign.
  • Use a root finder (root_bisect) to find the parameter where the error is zero. For the coffee: r ≈ 0.0115 per minute gives 70 °C after 30 minutes.

questions.q: If a patient's tissues respond weakly to insulin (insulin resistance), which parameter in the model would be small?

opts.t: k₃: insulin above basal produces only a little remote insulin X, so glucose falls slowly

questions.why: k₃ converts excess insulin into remote insulin X, which drives extra glucose uptake. Insulin sensitivity is defined as S_I = k₃/k₂.

questions.q: Why use an ODE solver instead of the Euler loop from chapter 17?

opts.t: Euler can't handle two state variables
The solver adapts its step size and uses better methods, so it's more accurate for the same work, and you only write the derivatives

questions.why: Euler with a fixed dt has an error that shrinks only in proportion to dt. Adaptive solvers (scipy's RK45 here) take small steps where things change fast and big ones where they don't, and they control the error for you.

questions.q: What's the difference between an update function and a slope function, and how do you fit a model's parameters?
questions.a:
• An update function computes the next state itself (e.g. an Euler step with fixed dt). A slope function only returns derivatives; the ODE solver decides how to step.
  • Fitting: write an error function returning model − data for given parameters; a least-squares optimiser (fit_leastsq) adjusts the parameters to minimise the sum of squared errors.

questions.q: Why is the RC filter mathematically the same kind of system as the cooling coffee?

opts.t: Both say the rate of change is proportional to the gap between the current value and a target (room temperature, input voltage)
They aren't the same; one is electrical

questions.why: dT/dt = −r(T − T_env) and dV/dt = (V_in − V)/(RC) have the same form, with r ↔ 1/RC. Spotting the same structure in different systems is one of the most useful modeling skills.

questions.q: Name three tools from Part II and say when you'd reach for each.
questions.a:
• run_ode_solver with a slope function: for any system described by differential equations.
  • interpolate: when a model needs a measured input at times between samples.
  • root_bisect / fit_leastsq: to find a parameter that hits a target, or the parameters that best match data.
  • (Also: SweepSeries/SweepFrame to see how results depend on parameters.)

questions.q: To simulate a falling object with run_ode_solver, what goes in the state?
questions.why: The slope function must return the derivative of every state variable. Position's derivative is velocity (which must therefore be in the state) and velocity's derivative is acceleration (computed from forces).

questions.q: How do we turn Newton's second law into something run_ode_solver can solve, and how does it stop at the ground?
questions.a:
• Use position and velocity as state variables: dy/dt = v, dv/dt = F/m (here −g). Two first-order ODEs instead of one second-order one.
  • An event function returns y; the solver stops when it crosses zero, so the last row of results is the moment of impact.

questions.q: If you double an object's speed, what happens to its drag force?

opts.t: Nothing; drag depends only on shape

questions.why: Drag is proportional to v², so 2× the speed gives 4× the force. That's why terminal velocity arrives fairly quickly for light objects.

questions.q: With drag, the penny takes about 22 s and hits at about 18 m/s, instead of 8.8 s and 86 m/s. What does that say about the myth?

opts.t: It's false: a penny reaches terminal velocity in a couple of seconds and lands at about 18 m/s, which stings but isn't deadly

questions.why: This closes the modeling loop from chapter 1: add the missing physics, re-predict, and the prediction agrees with measurement.

questions.q: What is terminal velocity, and how did we use it to find the penny's drag coefficient?
questions.a:
• The speed at which drag equals weight, so acceleration is zero and speed stops changing.
  • Setting ½ρv²C_dA = mg at the measured terminal velocity (18 m/s) gives C_d = 2mg/(ρAv²) ≈ 0.44 for a penny.

questions.q: Air resistance cuts the 45° hit from about 164 m to about 100 m. Which is also true of the trajectory with drag?

opts.t: It's lopsided: the ball comes down more steeply than it went up, because drag has slowed its horizontal motion
It goes higher than without air

questions.why: Without air the path is a symmetric parabola. Drag keeps removing horizontal speed, so the descent is steeper and shorter than the climb.

questions.q: How do you write drag for 2-D motion with Vectors?
questions.a:
• Magnitude ½ρ|V|²C_dA, same as 1-D.
  • Direction opposite to the velocity: multiply the magnitude by −V.hat().
  • Acceleration = gravity Vector(0, −g) + drag/mass; the slope function returns (V, A).

questions.q: Without air the best angle is exactly 45°. With drag the optimizer finds a smaller angle. Why does drag favour a flatter launch?

opts.t: A higher arc keeps the ball in the air longer, giving drag more time to slow it, so trading a little height for horizontal speed pays off
Gravity is weaker at lower angles

questions.why: Drag punishes time in flight. A slightly flatter trajectory spends less time losing speed, so the optimum moves below 45°.

questions.q: Describe the two-level search the Manny Ramirez problem uses.
questions.a:
• Inner: for a given speed, maximize searches over launch angle (each evaluation runs a full simulation) to find the best angle.
  • Outer: root_bisect searches over speed for the value where the ball's height at the wall, at its best angle, equals the wall's height.
  • Each level wraps a simulation in a function of one parameter, so standard optimizers and root finders can drive it.

questions.q: The final radius comes out at about 2.0 cm, the core radius, even though we never told the model to stop there. Why is that a good sign?

opts.t: k was derived from R_min, R_max and L; unrolling exactly L metres should bring the radius back to R_min, so the match checks the model's consistency
The event stops at the core

questions.why: The event stops when y = L. Landing on R_min at that moment confirms that the geometry (k) and the dynamics agree. Checks like this catch bugs.

questions.q: How does the toilet paper model connect rotation to linear motion?
questions.a:
• The rim moves at v = r·ω, so paper comes off at dy/dt = r·ω.
  • Each radian unrolled removes thickness k, so dr/dt = −k·ω with k = (R_max² − R_min²)/(2L).
  • With constant ω, θ grows steadily while the paper comes out more slowly as r shrinks; an event stops at y = L.

questions.q: Two disks have the same mass, but one has twice the radius. Compared with the smaller one, how much torque does it need for the same angular acceleration?
questions.why: I = ½mr², so doubling r quadruples I, and τ = Iα needs four times the torque. Mass far from the axis is hard to spin.

questions.q: State Newton's second law for rotation and the two moment-of-inertia formulas used here.
questions.a:
• τ = I·α: net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
  • Solid disk: I = ½mr². Point mass at distance r: I = mr². Moments of inertia add.
  • Simulate with state (θ, ω): dθ/dt = ω, dω/dt = τ/I.

questions.q: Why does the event for the lowest point need the condition t > 0.1?

opts.t: At the very start v = 0, which would trigger "velocity crosses zero" immediately; ignoring the first moment lets the jump happen
The cord isn't attached at t = 0

questions.why: The jumper starts at rest, so v is zero at t = 0. Returning a nonzero value for the first instant keeps the event from firing before anything happens.

questions.q: Walk through the steps you'd take to model a new physical system with the ModSim toolkit, using the bungee jump as the example.
questions.a:
• Choose state variables (height and velocity) and parameters (mass, cord length, k, terminal velocity), in State and Params/System objects.
  • Write a slope function from the forces (gravity, drag, spring) via Newton's second law.
  • Solve with run_ode_solver; use events to stop at meaningful moments (lowest point).
  • Wrap the run in a function of one parameter (k), then sweep it or use root_bisect / maximize to answer the design question.
  • Validate against reality where you can, and iterate.
